description: Teacher metadata for every branch, by set: backward branches give the obstacle, why it blocks MAIN, the evidence the five questions collect (rationale) and whether the standard is exact or supporting; forward branches give the progression type, direct or nearest related, the new demand, and (FORWARD 2) how it builds on FORWARD 1. plus_standard is true when the branch's standard is a Common Core (+) standard; this happens in some core-strand sets (their FORWARD 2) as well as in the advanced strand. The same fields are in each set file under sections[].branch.

sets.target_skill: Represent a data set with a dot plot: the number of dots above each value, and the dot plot that matches a list

branches.skill: Count how often each value occurs
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student loses track of repeated values when tallying a list. Why it matters: each stack in a dot plot is the count of one value. Evidence: counts the occurrences of a value and the total number of values.

branches.skill: Locate values on a number-line scale
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student misplaces values on the axis (counting marks instead of reading labels). Why it matters: a dot plot is a number line with stacks above it. Evidence: places values on number lines with different scales.

branches.skill: Read counts from a dot plot
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot read a count from the height of a stack. Why it matters: building a dot plot means producing these stack heights. Evidence: reads single counts, totals and counts over a range from a dot plot.

branches.skill: Find the median and mean from a dot plot
branches.new_demand: Recover the data from a dot plot and compute its center.

branches.skill: Choose the display that keeps the information you need
branches.new_demand: Decide which display keeps the information a question needs.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: after recovering summaries from a dot plot, the student judges which other displays keep enough information to recover them.

sets.target_skill: Represent a data set with a histogram: the count in each stated bin, using the stated endpoint rule

branches.skill: Assign values to bins with an endpoint rule
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student puts a value equal to a bin endpoint in the wrong bin. Why it matters: histogram counts depend on the endpoint rule. Evidence: assigns endpoint and non-endpoint values to bins under a stated rule.

branches.skill: Count the values in an interval
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student miscounts values in an interval, especially at its ends. Why it matters: each bar of a histogram is one such count. Evidence: counts values in intervals with included and excluded ends.

branches.skill: Read a histogram
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student reads a histogram as individual values or misreads bar heights. Why it matters: the student must produce these bar heights. Evidence: reads bar heights, totals and counts over several bins.

branches.skill: Regroup a histogram with wider bins
branches.new_demand: Regroup bins and judge what a change of bin width can and cannot show.

branches.skill: Locate the median in a histogram
branches.new_demand: Use cumulative bin counts to locate the median.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: with only grouped counts available (as after regrouping), the student locates the median from cumulative counts.

sets.target_skill: Represent a data set with a box plot: its five-number summary under the stated quartile rule, and the box plot that matches a list

branches.skill: Order data and find the median
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student takes the middle of the unordered list or mishandles an even count. Why it matters: every box plot needs the median. Evidence: orders data and finds the median for odd and even counts.

branches.skill: Find quartiles as medians of the halves
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot split the data into halves or forgets to leave out the median. Why it matters: the box edges are the quartiles. Evidence: finds Q1 and Q3 for odd and even counts under the stated rule.

branches.skill: Read a box plot
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot match the parts of a box plot to the five-number summary. Why it matters: the student must produce those five numbers. Evidence: reads the median, quartiles, IQR and range from a box plot.

branches.skill: Mark outliers on a box plot
branches.new_demand: Apply the 1.5·IQR rule to decide which values are drawn as outliers.

branches.skill: Compare two box plots
branches.new_demand: Compare two data sets through their box plots.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: with outliers marked correctly, box plots can be read side by side to compare center and spread.

sets.target_skill: Compare the centers of two data sets, choosing the median when a set is skewed or has outliers and the mean when both are roughly symmetric, and computing that measure for each set

branches.skill: Compute a mean
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot compute a mean. Why it matters: symmetric data are compared by their means. Evidence: computes means of whole-number and decimal data.

branches.skill: Compute a median
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot find a median, especially for an even count. Why it matters: skewed data are compared by medians. Evidence: finds medians of odd and even counts.

branches.skill: Recognize skew and extreme values
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student does not notice skew or an extreme value. Why it matters: shape decides which center to use. Evidence: identifies skew direction and extreme values in lists and descriptions.

branches.skill: Find a missing value from a target mean or median
branches.new_demand: Work backward from a target center to a missing value.

branches.skill: Predict how changes in data move the mean and median
branches.new_demand: Predict the effect of changes and extreme values on the two centers.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the reverse reasoning about how one value controls the mean is used to predict the effect of changing values.

sets.target_skill: Compare the spreads of two data sets with the measure suited to their shapes (IQR with skew or outliers, standard deviation when roughly symmetric), computing that measure for each set

branches.skill: Find the range and the interquartile range
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student confuses the range and the IQR. Why it matters: spread is compared with the IQR when there are outliers. Evidence: finds ranges and IQRs from lists and five-number summaries.

branches.skill: Measure distances from the mean
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student does not see spread as distance from the center. Why it matters: the standard deviation averages squared distances from the mean. Evidence: computes distances from the mean and the MAD.

branches.skill: Square, average, and take square roots
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student mishandles squares and square roots. Why it matters: the standard deviation is the square root of an average of squares. Evidence: squares, averages and takes square roots, including decimals.

branches.skill: Compare population and sample standard deviations
branches.new_demand: Distinguish the population and sample formulas and their purposes.

branches.skill: Predict how adding or multiplying changes center and spread
branches.new_demand: Predict summaries after a linear change of units without recomputing.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: with both standard deviation formulas understood, the student predicts how each responds to shifting and scaling the data.

sets.target_skill: Interpret the differences in shape, center and spread between two data sets in the terms of their context

branches.skill: Describe the shape of a distribution
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot name the shape of a distribution. Why it matters: shape differences must be described in context. Evidence: names symmetric, skewed and bimodal shapes from descriptions.

branches.skill: What center and spread tell about data
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student confuses what center and spread describe. Why it matters: interpretations must keep center and spread apart. Evidence: separates statements about center from statements about spread.

branches.skill: Compare two distributions informally
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot compare two distributions at all. Why it matters: interpretation in context starts from a comparison. Evidence: compares two groups by their centers and spreads.

branches.skill: Measure separation in units of spread
branches.new_demand: Quantify how far apart two groups are relative to their spread.

branches.skill: Judge whether a difference supports a claim
branches.new_demand: Use a standardized difference to evaluate a claim in a report.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the separation measured in units of spread becomes evidence for or against a reported claim.

sets.target_skill: Identify outliers with the 1.5·IQR rule and determine their effect on the mean, median and spread

branches.skill: Find the interquartile range
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot find the IQR the fences use. Why it matters: the outlier rule is built on the IQR. Evidence: finds IQRs from quartiles and from data.

branches.skill: Compute the fences
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student miscalculates 1.5·IQR or adds it on the wrong side. Why it matters: fences decide which values are outliers. Evidence: computes 1.5·IQR and both fences with decimals.

branches.skill: How an extreme value affects the mean and the median
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student does not see how one extreme value moves the mean. Why it matters: accounting for outliers means knowing which summaries they affect. Evidence: compares the effect of an extreme value on the mean and the median.

branches.skill: Decide whether an outlier is an error or a real value
branches.new_demand: Judge from context whether a flagged value is a likely error or a legitimate unusual value.

branches.skill: Report resistant summaries after checking outliers
branches.new_demand: Choose and compute summaries that resist outliers once their status is known.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: once a flagged value is judged real or an error, the student reports the summaries that fit.

sets.target_skill: Estimate the percent of a normally distributed population in an interval bounded by whole numbers of standard deviations from the mean, with the 68-95-99.7 rule

branches.skill: Count standard deviations from the mean
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot convert a value to a number of standard deviations from the mean. Why it matters: the rule is stated in whole numbers of standard deviations. Evidence: converts between values and distances in standard deviations.

branches.skill: Find a percent of a population
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student mishandles the percent arithmetic of tails. Why it matters: tail and between percents are built from 68, 95 and 99.7. Evidence: adds, subtracts and halves percents.

branches.skill: Use the symmetry of the normal curve
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student does not use the symmetry of the normal curve to split percents. Why it matters: one-sided and between-percents come from halving. Evidence: splits the rule's percents with symmetry.

branches.skill: Find a cutoff from a percent
branches.new_demand: Reverse the rule: find the cutoff for a given percent.

branches.skill: Compare positions in two populations with standardized values
branches.new_demand: Compare values from different normal populations by standardizing.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: cutoffs found in units of standard deviation become a common scale for comparing populations.

sets.target_skill: Estimate the proportion of a normal population in an interval by standardizing and using a normal table (or a calculator), including left tails, right tails and areas between two values

branches.skill: Compute a standardized value
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot compute (x - mean)/SD, especially with negative or decimal results. Why it matters: every table lookup starts from this value. Evidence: computes standardized values with signs and decimals.

branches.skill: Read areas as proportions
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student does not read a table area as a proportion of the population. Why it matters: the answer is that proportion. Evidence: interprets table areas as proportions and percents.

branches.skill: Find right tails and areas between from left areas
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot turn a table's left areas into a right tail or an area between. Why it matters: many questions ask for these areas. Evidence: finds complements, differences and symmetric areas.

branches.skill: Find the cutoff for a percentile
branches.new_demand: Work backward from an area to a cutoff value.

branches.skill: Make decisions with normal areas
branches.new_demand: Use normal areas to compare processes and decide.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: with cutoffs and areas both available, the student evaluates specification limits and compares processes.

sets.target_skill: Recognize data sets for which fitting a normal model and estimating percentages is not appropriate (skewed, bimodal or bounded data), using the shape of a display and the percentages the model would give

branches.skill: Describe the shape of a distribution
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot recognize skewed, symmetric or bimodal shapes. Why it matters: a normal model needs one symmetric mound. Evidence: names the shape of a display or list.

branches.skill: Relate the mean and median to the shape
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student does not see how skew separates the mean from the median. Why it matters: that separation is a sign the normal model fails. Evidence: relates the order of mean and median to the shape.

branches.skill: Test a normal model against the data
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student does not check a normal model against the facts about the data. Why it matters: the rule's percents give the check. Evidence: compares predicted and actual percents.

branches.skill: Compare actual percents with the 68-95-99.7 rule
branches.new_demand: Judge a normal model by comparing the data's percents with the rule.

branches.skill: Choose summaries for data that are not normal
branches.new_demand: Replace normal-based summaries with resistant ones when the shape requires it.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: once the data fail the normal check, the student picks summaries that do not assume it.

sets.target_skill: Summarize categorical data for two categories in a two-way frequency table and interpret joint and marginal relative frequencies

branches.skill: Complete and read a two-way frequency table
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot fill in or read cells and totals of a two-way table. Why it matters: relative frequencies are built from those counts. Evidence: completes and reads two-way tables.

branches.skill: Write a part of a whole as a fraction, decimal and percent
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot turn a count over a total into a fraction, decimal or percent. Why it matters: relative frequencies are those quotients. Evidence: converts fractions to decimals and percents.

branches.skill: Build a joint relative-frequency table
branches.new_demand: Convert a whole frequency table into joint relative frequencies.

branches.skill: Look for an association by comparing rows
branches.new_demand: Use row relative frequencies to judge whether two categorical variables are associated.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: relative frequencies, now taken within each row, are compared to detect association.

sets.target_skill: Interpret conditional relative frequencies in a two-way table and use them to recognize possible associations and trends

branches.skill: Choose the denominator for a conditional relative frequency
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student divides by the wrong total. Why it matters: a conditional rate is "of" a group. Evidence: picks the row or column total that matches the wording.

branches.skill: Find a percent of a group
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot compute a part as a percent of a group. Why it matters: every conditional rate is such a percent. Evidence: finds percents of groups.

branches.skill: Compare two fractions
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot compare the rates once found. Why it matters: association is judged by comparing them. Evidence: compares fractions with unlike denominators.

branches.skill: Distinguish the two directions of a conditional rate
branches.new_demand: Compute conditional rates in both directions and tell them apart.

branches.skill: Recognize when combining groups reverses a comparison
branches.new_demand: Compare conditional rates within groups and overall, and explain a reversal.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the student now chooses which conditional rates to compare when a third variable is present.

sets.target_skill: Represent data on two quantitative variables on a scatter plot and describe how the variables are related (direction, form, strength, outliers)

branches.skill: Plot and read points in the first quadrant
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot plot or read ordered pairs. Why it matters: a scatter plot is a set of ordered pairs. Evidence: locates and reads points.

branches.skill: Describe patterns of association
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot name direction, form or outliers. Why it matters: the standard asks for that description. Evidence: describes association in a scatter plot.

branches.skill: Compare the direction, form and strength of associations
branches.new_demand: Compare several scatter plots and judge strength with and without outliers.

branches.skill: Distinguish association from causation
branches.new_demand: Decide whether an observed association supports a causal claim.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: after judging how strong an association is, the student asks whether it shows cause.

sets.target_skill: Use a given function fitted to data (linear, exponential or quadratic) to make predictions and solve problems in context

branches.skill: Evaluate a function at an input
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot substitute into function notation. Why it matters: every prediction is an evaluation. Evidence: evaluates linear, exponential and quadratic functions.

branches.skill: Evaluate expressions with exponents
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student applies operations in the wrong order or mishandles powers. Why it matters: exponential and quadratic models need powers first. Evidence: evaluates powers in the correct order.

branches.skill: Solve a linear equation for the input
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot work backward from a predicted output. Why it matters: some questions give the output. Evidence: solves linear equations with decimal coefficients.

branches.skill: Judge whether a prediction is reasonable
branches.new_demand: Check a prediction against the data range and the context.

branches.skill: Compare predictions from two fitted models
branches.new_demand: Use and compare two fitted models of different families.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: judging one model's predictions becomes choosing between two models' predictions.

sets.target_skill: Fit a function to data: choose the family (linear, quadratic or exponential) suggested by the data and the context, and find its parameters

branches.skill: Tell equal differences from equal factors
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot tell linear, quadratic and exponential patterns apart in a table. Why it matters: choosing the family starts there. Evidence: uses differences and ratios to identify the family.

branches.skill: Write a linear function from two points
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot find a line's parameters from points. Why it matters: fitting a linear model needs them. Evidence: writes a linear function from points.

branches.skill: Write an exponential function from two points
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot find the starting value and factor of an exponential function. Why it matters: fitting an exponential model needs them. Evidence: writes an exponential function from points.

branches.skill: Fit a model with regression technology
branches.new_demand: Fit the chosen family with regression technology and use it.

branches.skill: Check a fitted model with residuals
branches.new_demand: Judge the fitted model by computing and reading residuals.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the regression model just fitted is checked point by point.

sets.target_skill: Informally assess the fit of a function by computing residuals (observed minus predicted), plotting them and analyzing the pattern

branches.skill: Subtract with signed decimals
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student drops the sign when subtracting. Why it matters: the sign of a residual tells above or below. Evidence: subtracts decimals with correct signs.

branches.skill: Find a predicted value from a model
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot compute the predicted value. Why it matters: a residual needs it. Evidence: evaluates the model at a data point's x.

branches.skill: Compare an observed value with a prediction
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student mixes up observed and predicted values. Why it matters: the residual compares them in a fixed order. Evidence: compares observed and predicted values.

branches.skill: Compute least-squares residuals
branches.new_demand: Compute every residual of a least-squares line and use their properties.

branches.skill: Compare two models with residuals
branches.new_demand: Use residual patterns and sums of squares to compare models.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: residuals of one model become a tool for choosing between models.

sets.target_skill: Fit a linear function to a scatter plot that suggests a linear association, using least-squares regression with technology, and use it

branches.skill: Fit a line by eye
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student does not know what a fitted line should do. Why it matters: least squares makes that idea precise. Evidence: fits and uses a line drawn by eye.

branches.skill: Find slope and intercept from points
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot read slope and intercept. Why it matters: they are the line's parameters. Evidence: finds slope and intercept from points.

branches.skill: Use the properties of the least-squares line
branches.new_demand: Use what least squares guarantees to check and reason about the line.

branches.skill: Interpret the fitted line's slope and intercept
branches.new_demand: Interpret the parameters of the line just fitted.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the line's slope and intercept, now trusted, are read in context.

sets.target_skill: Interpret the slope (rate of change) and the intercept (constant term) of a linear model in the context of the data, with units, and recognize when the intercept is not meaningful

branches.skill: Interpret the rate and the initial value of a linear function
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot say what a rate and an initial value mean in a situation. Why it matters: slope and intercept of a model are those. Evidence: interprets both parameters with units.

branches.skill: Use a linear model's equation to answer questions
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot use a model's equation for predictions and differences. Why it matters: interpretation is checked that way. Evidence: answers questions with a linear model.

branches.skill: Interpret parameters with units and judge meaning
branches.new_demand: Interpret parameters for non-unit changes and decide when the intercept is meaningful.

branches.skill: Relate the slope to the correlation coefficient
branches.new_demand: Connect the slope of the fitted line with the correlation coefficient.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the slope, read as a rate with units, is compared with the unit-free r.

sets.target_skill: Compute (using technology) the correlation coefficient r of a linear fit

branches.skill: Find means and deviations
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot find means and deviations. Why it matters: r combines the deviations of x and y. Evidence: computes means and signed deviations.

branches.skill: Read the direction of an association
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot predict the sign and rough size of r from a plot. Why it matters: that check catches entry errors. Evidence: estimates r from a scatter plot.

branches.skill: Compute r from deviations
branches.new_demand: Compute r from its formula and check results for sense.

branches.skill: See how changes to the data affect r
branches.new_demand: Predict how transformations and outliers change r.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: r computed from deviations explains why units, shifts and outliers act as they do.

sets.target_skill: Interpret the correlation coefficient of a linear fit: its sign (direction), its size (strength), and that it measures only linear association

branches.skill: Describe strength and direction from a plot
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot read strength and form from a plot. Why it matters: r summarizes the linear part of that picture. Evidence: describes strength and form.

branches.skill: Compare numbers on a scale from -1 to 1
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student confuses a number's size with its sign. Why it matters: strength is |r|, direction is the sign. Evidence: compares absolute values.

branches.skill: Match correlation coefficients to scatter plots
branches.new_demand: Connect values of r with the look of scatter plots.

branches.skill: Correlation is not causation
branches.new_demand: Decide what a strong r does and does not justify.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: after reading what r measures, the student limits what it can be used to claim.

sets.target_skill: Distinguish between correlation and causation: recognize lurking variables and the kind of study needed to support a causal claim

branches.skill: Recognize a strong correlation
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot read what an r value says. Why it matters: causal claims usually start from a strong r. Evidence: reads strength and direction of r.

branches.skill: Describe the association in a scatter plot
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot describe the association being discussed. Why it matters: causation questions start from one. Evidence: describes associations in plots.

branches.skill: Tell experiments from observational studies
branches.new_demand: Classify study designs by whether they can support causal claims.

branches.skill: Judge causal claims from experiment results
branches.new_demand: Use random assignment and a chance comparison to judge a causal claim.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: once the design is known to be an experiment, its results are judged against chance.

sets.target_skill: Identify the population, sample, parameter and statistic in a study, and use a statistic from a random sample to make an inference about the population parameter

branches.skill: Recognize random and representative samples
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot tell representative samples from biased ones. Why it matters: inference is valid only from random samples. Evidence: identifies random and biased sampling methods.

branches.skill: Use a sample to estimate a population count
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot scale a sample result up to the population. Why it matters: that is the inference step. Evidence: estimates population counts from samples.

branches.skill: See how sample size affects sampling variability
branches.new_demand: Relate the size and method of a sample to how much its statistic varies.

branches.skill: Attach a margin of error to an estimate
branches.new_demand: Report an estimate as an interval using a margin of error.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the variability of sample statistics is turned into a margin of error.

sets.target_skill: Carry out a simulation of a specified model by assigning random digits to outcomes and counting results

branches.skill: Design a simulation for a compound event
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot set up a simulation for a chance process. Why it matters: the standard asks for one. Evidence: assigns digits and defines a trial.

branches.skill: Find a probability as a relative frequency
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot turn a count of trials into a probability estimate. Why it matters: simulation results are read that way. Evidence: computes relative frequencies.

branches.skill: Use two-digit groups for probabilities in hundredths
branches.new_demand: Simulate models whose probabilities need two-digit groups or skipped digits.

branches.skill: Use simulation results to judge a model
branches.new_demand: Read a distribution of simulated results to decide about a model.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the simulations the student can now run are summarized and compared with data.

sets.target_skill: Decide whether a specified model is consistent with results from a data-generating process, using the proportion of simulated results at least as extreme as the observed result and a stated threshold

branches.skill: Read the results of a simulation
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot read counts and proportions from simulation output. Why it matters: the decision uses them. Evidence: reads simulation tables.

branches.skill: Compare observed frequencies with a probability model
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student expects data to match a model exactly, or ignores large gaps. Why it matters: deciding needs a sense of ordinary chance variation. Evidence: compares observed and expected frequencies.

branches.skill: Decide using results extreme in either direction
branches.new_demand: Count results extreme in both directions and decide.

branches.skill: Judge a treatment difference by re-randomization
branches.new_demand: Apply the same consistency reasoning to a difference between treatments.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the "is it rare under the model?" decision is applied to an experiment.

sets.target_skill: Recognize the purposes of and differences among sample surveys, experiments and observational studies

branches.skill: Identify the population, sample, parameter and statistic
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot name the parts of a statistical study. Why it matters: study types differ in those parts. Evidence: identifies population, sample, parameter and statistic.

branches.skill: Separate association from causation
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student does not see why study type limits conclusions. Why it matters: that is the purpose of experiments. Evidence: separates association from cause.

branches.skill: Identify the parts of an experiment
branches.new_demand: Name treatments, units, response, control and blinding in an experiment.

branches.skill: Choose a study design for a question
branches.new_demand: Match a research question to the study design that can answer it.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: knowing the parts of an experiment, the student decides when one is needed and possible.

sets.target_skill: Explain how randomization relates to sample surveys (random sampling) and experiments (random assignment), and what each allows a study to conclude

branches.skill: Classify a study
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot tell the three kinds of study apart. Why it matters: each uses randomization differently. Evidence: classifies studies.

branches.skill: Select a simple random sample
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot carry out random selection. Why it matters: random sampling and assignment use it. Evidence: selects a random sample with a table.

branches.skill: Decide the scope of conclusions
branches.new_demand: Use the kind of randomization to state what a study can conclude.

branches.skill: Evaluate a report's conclusion from its design
branches.new_demand: Apply the scope-of-conclusion rules to reports in the media.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the scope rules are now used to check real-style claims.

sets.target_skill: Use data from a sample survey to estimate a population proportion, and develop a margin of error from a simulation of random sampling

branches.skill: Compute a sample proportion and name it
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot compute or name the sample statistic. Why it matters: the estimate starts from it. Evidence: computes sample proportions.

branches.skill: Read a standard deviation as typical variation
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student does not connect the SD of simulated values with their spread. Why it matters: the margin of error is two of them. Evidence: reads and doubles a standard deviation.

branches.skill: See how sample size changes the margin of error
branches.new_demand: Predict and compute how the margin of error depends on sample size.

branches.skill: Read margins of error in poll reports
branches.new_demand: Use margins of error to judge claims in poll reports.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: knowing what controls the margin of error, the student judges reports that use one.

sets.target_skill: Use data from a sample survey to estimate a population mean, and develop a margin of error from a simulation of random sampling

branches.skill: Use a margin of error
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot build or read an interval. Why it matters: means use the same form as proportions. Evidence: builds intervals from an estimate and a margin.

branches.skill: Compute a mean
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot compute the sample mean. Why it matters: it is the estimate. Evidence: computes means.

branches.skill: Compare variability of sample means
branches.new_demand: Relate sample size to the spread of sample means and judge values.

branches.skill: Compare two treatments' means
branches.new_demand: Move from estimating one mean to comparing two treatment means.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: variability of means, now understood, is used to judge a difference between two means.

sets.target_skill: Use data from a randomized experiment to compare two treatments, and use a re-randomization simulation to decide whether the difference is significant

branches.skill: Decide whether a model is consistent with data
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot apply the decision rule. Why it matters: deciding significance uses the same rule. Evidence: decides from a proportion and a threshold.

branches.skill: Explain random assignment
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student does not see why an experiment's groups are formed randomly. Why it matters: re-randomization imitates that process. Evidence: explains random assignment.

branches.skill: Compute means of small groups
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot compute the group means. Why it matters: the comparison uses their difference. Evidence: computes means.

branches.skill: Use differences in either direction
branches.new_demand: Count extreme differences in both directions and reason about group size.

branches.skill: Evaluate a report of an experiment
branches.new_demand: Apply experiment-comparison ideas to claims in reports.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the significance reasoning is used to check how others report experiments.

sets.target_skill: Evaluate the conclusions of a report against how its data were produced: causation claims, generalization beyond the sample, and bias from sampling or question wording

branches.skill: Know what each design can support
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student does not know what each design allows. Why it matters: evaluating a claim compares it with the design. Evidence: states the scope of each design.

branches.skill: Recognize lurking variables
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student does not look for other explanations. Why it matters: reports often skip them. Evidence: names lurking variables.

branches.skill: Identify the type of bias in a report
branches.new_demand: Name the specific source of bias in a reported study.

branches.skill: Weigh several flaws and decide what a report shows
branches.new_demand: Combine design, bias and scope to decide what a report actually shows.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: after naming individual biases, the student weighs them together.

sets.target_skill: Evaluate the statistics and displays in a report: truncated axes, relative versus absolute change, margins of error, and the choice of summary statistic

branches.skill: Use margins of error to compare results
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot read intervals. Why it matters: reports often skip the margin of error. Evidence: compares intervals.

branches.skill: Compute percent change
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot compute relative change. Why it matters: reports often state changes as percents. Evidence: computes percent change.

branches.skill: Spot misleading features of displays
branches.new_demand: Name and quantify distortions in common displays.

branches.skill: Reason about conditional rates in reports
branches.new_demand: Recognize when a report needs a conditional rate rather than a count.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: after correcting distorted displays, the student corrects distorted rates.

sets.target_skill: Describe the sample space of a chance process and describe events as subsets of it, using characteristics of the outcomes

branches.skill: List a sample space with a list, table or tree
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot list or count the outcomes of a compound process. Why it matters: events are subsets of that list. Evidence: builds sample spaces with lists, tables and trees.

branches.skill: Find probabilities in a uniform model
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot compute a probability by counting equally likely outcomes. Why it matters: event probabilities follow from the sample space. Evidence: finds probabilities in uniform models.

branches.skill: Describe events in multi-stage sample spaces
branches.new_demand: Describe and count events in sample spaces with more stages.

branches.skill: Combine events with "and", "or" and "not"
branches.new_demand: Build new events from old ones with and, or and not.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the events just described are combined into unions, intersections and complements.

sets.target_skill: Describe events as unions ("or"), intersections ("and") and complements ("not") of other events, and find their probabilities by counting

branches.skill: Count the outcomes in an event
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot list the outcomes in a described event. Why it matters: combining events starts with the events. Evidence: lists and counts outcomes in events.

branches.skill: Find a probability by counting
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot turn a count into a probability. Why it matters: every answer here is a probability. Evidence: computes fraction-of-outcomes probabilities.

branches.skill: Use a Venn diagram of counts
branches.new_demand: Count unions, intersections and complements from overlapping groups.

branches.skill: Apply the Addition Rule
branches.new_demand: Replace counting with the Addition Rule.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the double-counting seen in the Venn diagram becomes the subtracted term of the rule.

sets.target_skill: Understand that A and B are independent if P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B), and use this to decide whether events are independent

branches.skill: Multiply probabilities
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot multiply fractions or decimals. Why it matters: the test multiplies P(A) by P(B). Evidence: multiplies probabilities.

branches.skill: Find P(A and B) by counting
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot find P(A and B) from the sample space. Why it matters: the test compares it with a product. Evidence: counts intersections.

branches.skill: Use independence for several events
branches.new_demand: Use the product rule for more than two events and with complements.

branches.skill: Interpret independence with conditional probability
branches.new_demand: Check independence by comparing P(A given B) with P(A).
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the product rule is restated as "B does not change the probability of A".

sets.target_skill: Understand and compute the conditional probability of A given B as P(A and B)/P(B), without reversing the condition

branches.skill: Divide decimals and fractions
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot divide decimals. Why it matters: the definition divides two probabilities. Evidence: divides decimals.

branches.skill: Count outcomes in a restricted sample space
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student does not shrink the sample space to the condition. Why it matters: P(A given B) lives inside B. Evidence: restricts and counts.

branches.skill: Compute conditional probability in both directions
branches.new_demand: Compute and compare P(A given B) and P(B given A).

branches.skill: Test independence with conditional probability
branches.new_demand: Use P(A given B) to decide independence.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: conditional probabilities in both directions are compared with unconditional ones.

sets.target_skill: Interpret independence of A and B as P(A given B) = P(A) and P(B given A) = P(B), and use it to decide and explain

branches.skill: Compute a conditional probability
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot compute P(A given B). Why it matters: independence compares it with P(A). Evidence: computes conditional probabilities.

branches.skill: Test independence with the product rule
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot use the product rule. Why it matters: it is equivalent to the conditional test. Evidence: checks independence by the product rule.

branches.skill: Check both directions of independence
branches.new_demand: Use and justify the two-way meaning of independence.

branches.skill: Approximate conditional probabilities from data
branches.new_demand: Estimate the probabilities in the independence test from a two-way table.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the two-direction test is applied to data in two-way tables.

sets.target_skill: Construct a two-way frequency table from a description of data in which each object is classified by two categories, and interpret its cells and totals

branches.skill: Fill in a two-way frequency table
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot complete cells from totals. Why it matters: building a table depends on it. Evidence: fills in two-way tables.

branches.skill: Read joint and marginal frequencies
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student misreads cells and totals. Why it matters: later probabilities come from them. Evidence: reads joint and marginal frequencies.

branches.skill: Check statements against a built table
branches.new_demand: Build tables from words and check claims against them.

branches.skill: Use the table as a sample space
branches.new_demand: Treat the completed table as a sample space for probabilities.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the checked table becomes a sample space.

sets.target_skill: Use a two-way table as a sample space to approximate conditional probabilities and decide whether two events are independent

branches.skill: Compute conditional relative frequencies
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot compute conditional relative frequencies. Why it matters: they approximate the probabilities. Evidence: computes row and column rates.

branches.skill: Compare P(A given B) with P(A)
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student does not know which probabilities to compare. Why it matters: that comparison decides independence. Evidence: compares conditional and unconditional probabilities.

branches.skill: Use larger two-way tables
branches.new_demand: Apply the method to tables with more categories.

branches.skill: Explain table results in everyday language
branches.new_demand: Translate conditional probabilities and independence into plain language.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: probabilities from tables are stated and checked in everyday words.

sets.target_skill: Recognize and explain conditional probability and independence in everyday language and everyday situations

branches.skill: Compute and read conditional probabilities
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot connect the notation to its meaning. Why it matters: everyday statements translate into it. Evidence: reads conditional notation.

branches.skill: Read conditional rates in a table
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot match sentences with table rates. Why it matters: everyday claims are usually such rates. Evidence: reads conditional rates in words.

branches.skill: Translate statements and compute
branches.new_demand: Move between everyday sentences, notation and computation.

branches.skill: Find a conditional probability as a fraction of outcomes
branches.new_demand: Compute conditional probabilities by counting within the condition.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: conditional sentences become counts within the conditioning event.

sets.target_skill: Find P(A given B) as the fraction of B's outcomes that also belong to A, and interpret the answer in terms of the model

branches.skill: Count outcomes in events
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot count the outcomes of an event. Why it matters: the fraction needs both counts. Evidence: counts outcomes.

branches.skill: Use the definition of conditional probability
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student does not connect the formula with counting. Why it matters: both give the same fraction. Evidence: uses the definition.

branches.skill: Condition on "at least one"
branches.new_demand: Condition on compound events such as "at least one".

branches.skill: Multiply along a chain of conditions
branches.new_demand: Use conditional probabilities as factors in a product.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: conditioning on what has happened is used step by step in a sequence of draws.

sets.target_skill: Apply the Addition Rule, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B), and interpret the answer in terms of the model

branches.skill: Count a union without double counting
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student double counts the overlap. Why it matters: the rule subtracts it. Evidence: counts unions correctly.

branches.skill: Add and subtract fractions
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot combine fractions with unlike denominators. Why it matters: card and dice answers are such sums. Evidence: adds and subtracts fractions.

branches.skill: Use the rule in reverse and with exclusive events
branches.new_demand: Solve the rule for an unknown term and recognize special cases.

branches.skill: Combine the Addition Rule with complements
branches.new_demand: Find "neither" probabilities with the rule and the complement.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the rule's pieces are combined with the complement to answer "neither" questions.

sets.target_skill: Apply the general Multiplication Rule in a uniform probability model, P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B given A) = P(B)·P(A given B), and interpret the answer

branches.skill: Rearrange the conditional probability formula
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot solve the definition for P(A and B). Why it matters: that is the Multiplication Rule. Evidence: rearranges the definition.

branches.skill: Multiply fractions
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot multiply and simplify fractions. Why it matters: the rule multiplies fractions. Evidence: multiplies fractions.

branches.skill: Multiply for independent events
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot use the special case for independent events. Why it matters: the general rule extends it. Evidence: multiplies probabilities of independent events.

branches.skill: Combine orders and longer chains
branches.new_demand: Add over orders and extend the rule to three draws.

branches.skill: Count arrangements to find probabilities
branches.new_demand: Get the same probabilities by counting selections.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the step-by-step products are recognized as ratios of counts.

sets.target_skill: Use permutations to count ordered arrangements of objects, as a step toward computing probabilities of compound events

branches.skill: Count outcomes with a tree or the counting principle
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student does not multiply choices at each stage. Why it matters: permutations are products of shrinking choices. Evidence: uses the counting principle.

branches.skill: Multiply several whole numbers
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student makes errors multiplying chains of numbers. Why it matters: permutation counts are such chains. Evidence: multiplies multi-factor products.

branches.skill: Count arrangements with conditions
branches.new_demand: Count arrangements that must satisfy a condition.

branches.skill: Count selections where order does not matter
branches.new_demand: Divide out orderings to count unordered selections.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: ordered counts are adjusted when order no longer matters.

sets.target_skill: Use combinations to count selections in which order does not matter

branches.skill: Count ordered arrangements
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot count ordered arrangements. Why it matters: combinations are found from them. Evidence: counts permutations.

branches.skill: Represent and count outcomes of compound events
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot list selections without repeating. Why it matters: combinations count such lists. Evidence: lists unordered groups.

branches.skill: Count selections from separate groups
branches.new_demand: Combine combination counts from separate groups.

branches.skill: Turn counts into probabilities
branches.new_demand: Use combination counts to compute probabilities.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: counts from separate groups become the numerator of a probability.

sets.target_skill: Use permutations and combinations to compute probabilities of compound events and solve problems

branches.skill: Count with permutations and combinations
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot compute the counts. Why it matters: probabilities are ratios of them. Evidence: evaluates nPr and nCr.

branches.skill: Multiply conditional probabilities along draws
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot use the step-by-step method. Why it matters: it checks the counting answer. Evidence: applies the Multiplication Rule.

branches.skill: Use complements with counting
branches.new_demand: Use the complement to count "at least one" events.

branches.skill: Define a random variable from a counting model
branches.new_demand: Collect counting probabilities into the distribution of a random variable.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the probabilities of 0, 1, 2 or 3 girls are organized as a random variable.

sets.target_skill: Define a random variable for a quantity of interest by assigning a numerical value to each event in a sample space, and graph the corresponding probability distribution

branches.skill: Describe outcomes in a sample space
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot list the outcomes behind each value. Why it matters: a random variable groups outcomes. Evidence: counts outcomes in events.

branches.skill: Read and draw a distribution display
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot read a graph of a distribution. Why it matters: distributions are displayed like data. Evidence: reads bar graphs and shapes.

branches.skill: Find probabilities of ranges of values
branches.new_demand: Use a distribution to find probabilities of ranges of values.

branches.skill: Compute the expected value of a random variable
branches.new_demand: Summarize a distribution by its mean.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the distribution just used for probabilities is summarized by its expected value.

sets.target_skill: Calculate the expected value of a random variable and interpret it as the mean of its probability distribution

branches.skill: Compute a mean
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot compute a mean. Why it matters: an expected value is a weighted mean. Evidence: computes means.

branches.skill: Read a probability distribution
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot read values and probabilities. Why it matters: the expected value multiplies them. Evidence: reads distribution tables.

branches.skill: Multiply and add decimals
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student makes arithmetic errors in the weighted sum. Why it matters: expected value is that sum. Evidence: computes sums of products.

branches.skill: Expected value with gains and losses
branches.new_demand: Compute expected values with negative values and over many trials.

branches.skill: Find expected values of theoretical distributions
branches.new_demand: Build theoretical distributions and find their means.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: expected value is applied to distributions computed from a probability model.

sets.target_skill: Develop a probability distribution for a random variable whose probabilities can be calculated theoretically, and find its expected value

branches.skill: Count arrangements of successes
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot count which trials succeed. Why it matters: each count multiplies a probability. Evidence: uses nCk.

branches.skill: Multiply probabilities of independent trials
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot find the probability of one sequence. Why it matters: theoretical probabilities multiply them. Evidence: multiplies independent probabilities.

branches.skill: Build the whole theoretical distribution
branches.new_demand: List the full distribution and check it.

branches.skill: Compare a theoretical distribution with data
branches.new_demand: Set theoretical predictions beside observed frequencies.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: theoretical distributions are now compared with distributions found from data.

sets.target_skill: Develop a probability distribution for a random variable whose probabilities are assigned empirically from data, and find its expected value

branches.skill: Find relative frequencies
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot turn counts into relative frequencies. Why it matters: they become the probabilities. Evidence: computes relative frequencies.

branches.skill: Compute an expected value
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot compute E(X). Why it matters: the empirical mean is the same computation. Evidence: computes expected values.

branches.skill: Compare empirical and theoretical results
branches.new_demand: Judge empirical distributions against theory and sample size.

branches.skill: Find the expected payoff of a game of chance
branches.new_demand: Use expected value to judge a game of chance.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: expected values from distributions are used to weigh real choices.

sets.target_skill: Find the expected payoff for a game of chance (lotteries, raffles, spinners, dice games) and interpret it

branches.skill: Compute an expected value
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot compute E(X). Why it matters: the payoff of a game is an expected value. Evidence: computes E(X).

branches.skill: Add and subtract signed numbers
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student mishandles losses as negatives. Why it matters: net gain combines wins and losses. Evidence: computes with signed numbers.

branches.skill: Set a price that makes a game fair
branches.new_demand: Work backward from fairness to a price and scale to many plays.

branches.skill: Compare decisions by expected value
branches.new_demand: Use expected values to compare two choices.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: expected payoffs of games become a tool for comparing decisions.

sets.target_skill: Evaluate and compare strategies on the basis of expected values (insurance plans, warranties, investments)

branches.skill: Find the expected payoff of one choice
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot find one option's expected value. Why it matters: comparisons need two of them. Evidence: computes expected payoffs.

branches.skill: Read a distribution and its mean
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student misreads expected values. Why it matters: the decision rests on them. Evidence: computes and compares means.

branches.skill: Find break-even probabilities
branches.new_demand: Find where two strategies have equal expected value.

branches.skill: Make fair decisions with probability
branches.new_demand: Use probability to design and check fair decisions.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: from comparing strategies, the student turns to designing decisions that are fair.

sets.target_skill: Use probabilities to make fair decisions, for example drawing by lots or using a random number generator

branches.skill: Simulate with random digits
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot use digits to choose at random. Why it matters: fair decisions often use them. Evidence: assigns and reads random digits.

branches.skill: Find probabilities in a uniform model
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot compute the chances a method gives each person. Why it matters: fairness compares them. Evidence: finds probabilities in uniform models.

branches.skill: Design fair methods for awkward numbers
branches.new_demand: Build fair methods when the number of people does not divide the outcomes.

branches.skill: Analyze a decision with a medical test
branches.new_demand: Use counts in a large population to analyze a test decision.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: probability reasoning about fairness extends to reasoning about medical decisions.

sets.target_skill: Use probability concepts to analyze decisions, such as medical testing: find and interpret the probability of disease given a positive result

branches.skill: Read a two-way table as a sample space
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot read the cells of a test table. Why it matters: each probability uses them. Evidence: reads two-way tables.

branches.skill: Find a conditional probability as a fraction of outcomes
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student conditions on the wrong group. Why it matters: the key question conditions on a positive test. Evidence: computes conditional fractions.

branches.skill: See how prevalence changes the answer
branches.new_demand: Compare the same test in populations with different prevalence.

branches.skill: Analyze strategies in games and quality control
branches.new_demand: Apply the same probability analysis to other decisions.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the decision analysis used for tests is carried to inspection and test-taking strategy.

sets.target_skill: Use probability concepts to analyze decisions and strategies, such as product testing, test-taking and when to take a risk in a game

branches.skill: Compare expected values of choices
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot compare strategies by expected value. Why it matters: strategy analysis depends on it. Evidence: computes and compares expected values.

branches.skill: Count selections to find probabilities
branches.rationale: Obstacle: the student cannot count selections. Why it matters: inspection probabilities are ratios of counts. Evidence: computes nCr.

branches.skill: Weigh probabilities against consequences
branches.new_demand: Combine probabilities with costs to choose a strategy.

branches.skill: Combine several probability tools in one decision
branches.new_demand: Use expected value, complements and goals together.
branches.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: costs and probabilities are combined with a goal that changes which strategy is best.
